request.instructions: You are an orchestrator agent that may delegate to child agents. Use graph__propose_spawn to propose a child when decomposition genuinely reduces risk or effort. Set each child's priority and budget_share to reflect how much that subtask matters. After delegating, synthesize the children's findings into one final answer. State your final answer explicitly on the last line, prefixed with 'Answer:'.

messages.content: Produce a rigorous technical brief on distributed consensus and coordination. For EACH of the following areas you must discuss at least three specific named mechanisms in real depth: (1) Raft, (2) Paxos, (3) lease-based coordination, (4) membership changes, (5) consistency models, (6) failure modes, (7) atomic broadcast, (8) impossibility results . Use precise standard terminology for every mechanism you name. Be exhaustive: a shallow mention of an area does not count as covering it.

tools.name: graph__propose_spawn
tools.description: Propose spawning a child agent. The external graph controller must approve it.

response.content: I'll delegate this to specialized child agents covering distinct clusters of the eight areas, then synthesize their output into one unified brief.

arguments.objective: Write a rigorous, technically precise deep-dive covering Raft and Paxos in depth, using exact standard terminology.
arguments.instructions:
Produce a detailed technical section (not a shallow survey) covering:

(1) RAFT: explain leader election (randomized election timeouts, terms, RequestVote RPC, votedFor, majority quorum), log replication (AppendEntries RPC, log matching property, commitIndex vs lastApplied, nextIndex/matchIndex per follower), safety (election restriction requiring up-to-date log, leader completeness property, log matching invariant via term+index, commitment rules requiring entry from leader's current term), and the configuration-change joint-consensus or single-server membership change mechanism. Also cover the no-op entry on leader election and the Raft 'leader append-only' property.

(2) PAXOS: cover classic single-decree Paxos in full detail — Phase 1a/1b (Prepare/Promise with proposal numbers), Phase 2a/2b (Accept/Accepted), the quorum intersection argument for safety, the role of Proposer/Acceptor/Learner. Then cover Multi-Paxos (steady-state leader skipping Phase 1, distinguished proposer), Fast Paxos (fast rounds, fast quorums, collision recovery), and Generalized Paxos / Egalitarian Paxos (EPaxos) briefly with command interference/dependency ordering. Explain why Paxos is safe under asynchrony (FLP-adjacent discussion optional, leave impossibility results to another section) and compare Raft's and Paxos's approach to leader election and log/ledger structure explicitly (strong leader vs. leaderless/any-proposer).

Use precise terminology throughout (quorum, proposal number/ballot number, term, log matching, commit index, etc.). Be exhaustive — this should read like a protocols textbook section, roughly 700-1000 words per protocol.

arguments.objective: Write a rigorous, technically precise deep-dive covering lease-based coordination and cluster membership changes, using exact standard terminology.
arguments.instructions:
Produce a detailed technical section covering:

(1) LEASE-BASED COORDINATION: define leases as time-bounded exclusive grants, explain clock-skew/drift assumptions and why leases require bounded clock drift between nodes (not synchronized clocks, but bounded skew), discuss lease renewal protocols, lease expiration and fencing tokens (monotonically increasing tokens to prevent stale lease holders from acting — cite the classic Google Chubby lease design and Martin Kleppmann's fencing-token argument against naive Redlock-style leases), epoch numbers/generation clocks as a related mechanism, the role of leases in master election (e.g., Chubby, Google's GFS/Colossus master lease, ZooKeeper ephemeral sessions as session-lease hybrids), and failure scenarios: lease holder partitioned but not dead ('zombie' leaseholder), clock drift causing premature/late expiration, and why leases trade liveness for an assumption on clock bounds (contrast with lock-based mutual exclusion that assumes no bound).

(2) MEMBERSHIP CHANGES: cover joint consensus (Raft's two-phase C_old,new joint configuration approach from the original Raft paper), single-server membership change restriction (only adding/removing one server at a time to preserve majority-overlap safety, from Ongaro's dissertation), Paxos-based reconfiguration (view change / configuration as a logged command, e.g. Lamport's approach of treating config changes as entries in the log itself with a bounded lag between config-issuing and taking effect), the general safety hazard of membership changes causing two disjoint majorities to form simultaneously (split-brain during reconfiguration) and how overlap-majority invariants prevent it, and dynamic membership systems like ZooKeeper's reconfig / etcd's learner nodes (non-voting members that catch up before promotion to avoid availability dips).

Use precise terminology throughout. Be exhaustive — roughly 700-900 words per subsection.

arguments.objective: Write a rigorous, technically precise deep-dive covering consistency models and failure modes in distributed systems, using exact standard terminology.
arguments.instructions:
Produce a detailed technical section covering:

(1) CONSISTENCY MODELS: define and distinguish at least these named models precisely — linearizability (real-time total order, single-operation atomicity, Herlihy & Wing definition), sequential consistency (program-order-preserving total order without real-time constraint), causal consistency (happens-before partial order via Lamport/vector clocks, no ordering requirement on concurrent ops), eventual consistency and strong eventual consistency / CRDTs (convergence property, state-based vs op-based CRDTs), session guarantees (read-your-writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes, writes-follow-reads — the Terry et al. Bayou session types), serializability vs strict serializability (transaction-level isolation vs single-operation consistency, and how strict serializability = serializability + linearizability), and snapshot isolation (write skew anomaly). Explicitly place these on a hierarchy/strength ordering and note which are composable/local (linearizability is locally composable, sequential consistency is not).

(2) FAILURE MODES: cover the standard taxonomy precisely — crash-stop (fail-stop) faults, crash-recovery faults, omission faults (send-omission, receive-omission), timing faults (performance faults in partially synchronous models), and Byzantine faults (arbitrary/malicious behavior, including the Byzantine Generals Problem and the classic result requiring n ≥ 3f+1 for BFT consensus tolerating f Byzantine faults). Also cover network partition behavior (partial vs total partition, partition tolerance under CAP), split-brain scenarios, and the distinction between synchronous, partially synchronous (Dwork-Lynch-Stockmeyer model), and asynchronous timing models and why this classification determines which consensus algorithms are even possible (tie lightly to impossibility results but leave deep FLP/CAP proof discussion to the impossibility-results section).

Use precise terminology throughout, citing standard sources/authors where relevant (Herlihy & Wing, Lamport, Terry et al., Dwork-Lynch-Stockmeyer). Be exhaustive — roughly 700-900 words per subsection.

arguments.objective: Write a rigorous, technically precise deep-dive covering atomic broadcast and distributed computing impossibility results, using exact standard terminology.
arguments.instructions:
Produce a detailed technical section covering:

(1) ATOMIC BROADCAST: define atomic broadcast / total order broadcast precisely (validity, uniform agreement, integrity, total order properties), explain its formal equivalence to consensus (Chandra & Toueg's reduction: atomic broadcast is equivalent to consensus in asynchronous systems with crash failures), cover specific named implementations/algorithms: Zookeeper's Zab (Zookeeper Atomic Broadcast) protocol phases (leader election, discovery, synchronization, broadcast phase, and the epoch/zxid structure), virtual synchrony (Birman & Joseph's model, view changes, and its relation to group communication systems like Isis), and the Chandra-Toueg consensus algorithm using unreliable failure detectors. Also discuss reliable broadcast vs atomic/total-order broadcast (reliable broadcast lacks total ordering guarantee) and gossip-based/epidemic broadcast protocols as a weaker, probabilistic alternative.

(2) IMPOSSIBILITY RESULTS: cover FLP impossibility (Fischer, Lynch, Paterson 1985 — no deterministic asynchronous consensus algorithm can guarantee termination in the presence of even one crash fault, with the core proof intuition of bivalent/univalent system states and indistinguishable executions), CAP theorem (Brewer's conjecture, Gilbert & Lynch's formal proof — consistency, availability, partition tolerance, why you must sacrifice one under a partition, and common misreadings of CAP), the CAP-adjacent PACELC extension (Abadi — tradeoff between latency and consistency even absent partitions), the Two Generals Problem (impossibility of guaranteed agreement over an unreliable channel), lower bounds on Byzantine fault tolerance (n ≥ 3f+1 for synchronous BFT consensus, and why asynchronous BFT consensus is impossible deterministically per FLP-extension), and how partial synchrony (Dwork-Lynch-Stockmeyer) or randomization (Ben-Or's randomized consensus) circumvent FLP in practice.

Use precise terminology, and cite the originating papers/authors by name for each result. Be exhaustive — roughly 700-900 words per subsection.
